title: How to start a thread with the loop start
subtitle: A knotless thread start for even-numbered strand counts
excerpt: The loop start is a knotless method of beginning a new thread. It works only when stitching with an even number of strands — two, four, or six. A single thread is folded in half and the folded end is used as an anchor; the first stitch locks the loop securely and the thread start is invisible from the front.
sourceNotes: Loop start technique for cross-stitch. Widely documented in cross-stitch technique guides. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: The loop start creates a knotless anchor at the beginning of a thread. Because it relies on a fold, it only works with an even number of strands. To stitch with 2 strands using the loop start, separate a single strand of
to twice the usual working length (about 80–90 cm for a single strand), fold it in half, and thread the needle with the two ends rather than the fold.

Separate one strand of floss from the skein. This should be approximately twice the length you would normally use for a 2-strand working length. Fold the strand exactly in half so the two cut ends meet. Thread both cut ends through the eye of the needle; the folded end forms a loop at the other end of the thread.
Bring the needle up through the
at the position for the first leg of the first cross. Pull through, leaving the loop below the fabric.

Insert the needle down through the next hole of the Aida to complete the first leg of the cross, then bring the needle up through the loop at the back of the fabric. Pull the thread through, and the loop catches around the first leg of the stitch, anchoring the thread securely with no knot.

Continue stitching normally. The loop start should hold firm even after the first stitch. Check from the back that the loop is secure before moving more than a few stitches away from the starting point.

items.symptom: The loop comes undone after the first few stitches
items.cause: The needle was passed through the loop but the loop was not pulled snug around the first thread leg before continuing.
items.fix: Before stitching further, pull the two working strands firmly from the front of the fabric to tighten the loop anchor at the back. The loop should grip the thread leg without any slack. If it still comes loose, use a standard weave-in start instead.

items.symptom: There is a small lump visible on the front of the first stitch
items.cause: The loop pulled forward through the fabric hole and caught on the front.
items.fix: Pull the working thread back so the loop sits flat on the back of the fabric, not between the fabric layers. The loop should be entirely behind the Aida, not embedded in it.

content.text: The loop start only works for even strand counts. For 3-strand work or when stitching with an odd number of strands, use the standard weave-in start. Many stitchers use the loop start for all 2-strand work once they learn it, as it is faster than weaving in the tail and leaves a flatter back.
